quote: not by a term in the utility function for some other mind’s “desire,” but by the simpler and yet far more consequential path of mirror neurons
content: The mirror-neuron account of sympathy was fashionable in 2009 and hasn't held up. Mirror neurons were found in macaque premotor cortex and have some single-cell support in humans (Mukamel et al. 2010). But the leap from motor mirroring to understanding actions, let alone to empathy and sympathy, was criticized as unsupported (Hickok 2009), and the related "broken mirror" theory of autism fared poorly. The essay's account of why humans are sympathetic rests on a mechanism the field no longer credits with that role.

quote: The only possible way you can hit on an “Aha!” that describes a system as incredibly complex as an Other Mind, is if you happen to run across something amazingly similar to the Other Mind—namely your own brain
content: This was already one side of a long debate, simulation theory versus theory-theory. Brain imaging separates a mentalizing network, used to infer others' goals and beliefs, from the mirror system used for actions (Van Overwalle & Baetens 2009). The claim has since been undercut directly. A model fine-tuned on data from 160 psychology experiments predicts human choices in new tasks better than purpose-built cognitive models (Binz et al. 2025), with no human brain in the loop. Humans do use empathy, but it is not "the only possible way."

quote: You could, perhaps, have a specific urge to bring your allies food, like a vampire bat—they have a whole system of reciprocal blood donations going in those colonies.
content: This example holds up well. Wilkinson's 1984 field study documented food sharing among vampire bats. Later controlled work found that help previously received predicts donations more strongly than relatedness does (Carter & Wilkinson 2013). It remains one of the best-supported cases of reciprocity in a non-human mammal.

quote: There are cultures that help strangers… and cultures that eat strangers; the question is which of these requires the explicit imperative
content: The developmental evidence gives a mixed answer. Toddlers spontaneously help unfamiliar adults reach objects (Warneken & Tomasello 2006), which supports sympathy being "on by default." But costly sharing develops later. In middle childhood it diverges across societies as children converge on local adult norms (House et al. 2013), and it becomes more parochial with age (Fehr, Bernhard & Rockenbach 2008). "On by default, then tuned by culture" is closer to the evidence than either the essay's hunch or its opposite, and most of the variation comes from the tuning.

quote: “Happiness” is an idiom of policy reinforcement learning, not expected utility maximization.
content: This distinction doesn't do the work asked of it. A reinforcement learner maximizes expected cumulative reward, which makes it an expected utility maximizer over returns, and nothing about RL implies feeling anything. In the brain, the learning signal (dopaminergic prediction error, "wanting") is separable from hedonic pleasure ("liking") (Berridge & Robinson 1998). So neither RL nor its absence settles whether an agent feels happiness. Whether a paperclip maximizer would feel anything is a question about consciousness, and the algorithmic distinction doesn't reach it.

quote: natural selection, which doesn’t bother to anesthetize fatally wounded and dying creatures
content: Selection did install anesthesia for the wounded. Stress-induced analgesia, mediated by the body's own opioids and cannabinoids, suppresses pain during acute injury and extreme threat across mammals, so that an injured animal can fight or flee (Butler & Finn 2009). Reports of people and animals feeling little pain from severe wounds are common. The image of evolution leaving the dying in agony is rhetorically useful, and it returns in "The Gift We Give to Tomorrow," but the biology is more complicated than the rhetoric.
